items.title: Metrics, logs, traces
items.context: Metrics are cheap numeric time series for dashboards and alerts. Logs are detailed event records. Traces follow one request across services as a tree of timed spans. Together they let you go from 'something is wrong' to 'where and why'.

questions.prompt: Which signal shows that a request spent 800 ms waiting on the payment service?
questions.explanation: Each span records its service, operation and duration.

items.title: Prometheus basics
items.context: Prometheus scrapes (pulls) metrics over HTTP from /metrics endpoints at an interval and stores them as time series with labels. Counters only go up, so you query them with rate(): rate(http_requests_total[5m]) is the per-second average increase over the last 5 minutes.

choices: The total number of requests ever
The per-second request rate averaged over the last 5 minutes
questions.explanation: rate() also handles counter resets when a process restarts.

questions.prompt: Which metric type fits 'current queue length'?
questions.explanation: Gauges go up and down; counters only increase.

items.title: RED and USE
items.context: RED is for request-driven services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE is for resources (CPU, disks, pools): Utilisation, Saturation, Errors. They give a standard first dashboard for anything.

questions.prompt: For an HTTP API, the RED method tracks:
questions.explanation: Use USE for the database's connection pool or the node's disks.

items.title: SLI, SLO, SLA, error budget
items.context: An SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. the share of requests served under 300 ms). An SLO is the internal target (99.9% over 30 days). An SLA is an external contract with penalties. The error budget is the allowed failure: 100% − SLO. When it's spent, reliability work takes priority over features.

questions.prompt: With a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days, roughly how much downtime is in the error budget?

items.title: Alerting
items.context: Page on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency, SLO burn rate), not on every cause (CPU at 80%). Every page should be actionable and urgent; everything else goes to tickets or dashboards. Noisy alerts cause alert fatigue, and real incidents get ignored.

questions.prompt: Which alert deserves to wake someone at 3 a.m.?
choices: Checkout error rate is burning the monthly SLO budget fast
questions.explanation: Alert on user impact; investigate causes on dashboards.

items.title: Latency percentiles
items.context: Averages hide outliers. p50 is the median; p99 is the latency 99% of requests stay under. Users who make many requests hit the tail often, so SLOs usually target p95 or p99. Percentiles can't be averaged across instances; aggregate histograms instead.

questions.prompt: Average latency is 120 ms but users complain about slowness. Look at:
questions.explanation: One slow dependency call can sit in the tail while the average looks fine.

items.title: Structured logging
items.context: Write logs as structured key-value data (JSON) with a consistent schema — timestamp, level, service, trace_id, user_id — so they can be indexed and queried in Loki or Elasticsearch. Include a correlation or trace ID to join logs across services.

questions.prompt: What lets you find every log line from one request across five services?
choices: A shared correlation / trace ID in each log entry
questions.explanation: OpenTelemetry propagates the trace context automatically.

items.title: Tracing & OpenTelemetry
items.context: OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard (APIs, SDKs, a collector) for traces, metrics and logs. Trace context travels between services in the W3C traceparent header, so spans from different services join into one trace.

questions.prompt: How does service B know it's part of the trace started in service A?
choices: Both log to the same file
A passes the trace context in a header such as traceparent
questions.explanation: Auto-instrumentation libraries inject and extract the header for you.

items.title: Blameless postmortems
items.context: After an incident, write a blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, root and contributing causes, what went well, and concrete action items with owners. The focus is on systems and processes, not individuals, so people report problems honestly.

questions.prompt: The goal of a blameless postmortem is to:
choices: Find systemic fixes so the incident doesn't recur
questions.explanation: If a human could make the mistake, the system allowed it.

items.title: Grafana's role
items.context: Grafana visualises and alerts on data from other systems (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch); it doesn't store metrics itself. A common open-source stack is Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo or Jaeger for traces, and Grafana on top.

questions.prompt: In a Prometheus + Grafana setup, metrics are stored in:
questions.explanation: Grafana queries the data source on each dashboard load.

items.title: Label cardinality
items.context: Every unique combination of labels creates a separate time series. A label like user_id or request_id creates millions of series and can overload Prometheus. Keep labels bounded (method, status code, route template); put high-cardinality details in logs or traces.

questions.prompt: Which label is likely to blow up your metrics storage?
questions.explanation: Bounded labels have a small fixed set of values.

items.title: Synthetic monitoring vs RUM
items.context: Synthetic checks run scripted probes from outside on a schedule (is login working from 3 regions?), catching outages even with no traffic. Real User Monitoring measures what actual users experience in their browsers. Use both.

questions.prompt: Which detects that checkout is broken at 4 a.m. when no customers are active?
questions.explanation: RUM needs real users to report anything.

items.title: MTTD and MTTR
items.context: MTTD (mean time to detect) and MTTR (mean time to recover/restore) measure incident response. Good alerting reduces MTTD; runbooks, quick rollbacks and good observability reduce MTTR.

questions.prompt: Faster rollbacks and good runbooks mainly improve:
questions.explanation: Often more achievable than preventing every failure.

items.title: Burn-rate alerts
items.context: Burn rate is how fast you're consuming the error budget relative to the SLO: a burn rate of 1 spends it exactly over the SLO window; 14.4 spends a 30-day budget in about 2 days. Multi-window burn-rate alerts page for fast burns and open tickets for slow ones.

choices: The error budget will be used up exactly at the end of the SLO window
questions.explanation: Higher numbers mean faster budget consumption.

items.title: Black-box vs white-box monitoring
items.context: Black-box monitoring tests from outside like a user (HTTP probes, synthetic checks): it shows that something is broken. White-box monitoring uses internals (metrics, logs, traces): it shows why. You need both.

questions.prompt: Prometheus scraping your app's internal queue-depth metric is:
questions.explanation: An external HTTP probe would be black-box.

items.title: Runbooks & on-call
items.context: Every alert should link to a runbook: what it means, how to check impact, and the first steps to mitigate. Sustainable on-call means a fair rotation, actionable pages only, and follow-up work to remove recurring causes.

questions.prompt: What should every paging alert include?
choices: Nothing; on-call should figure it out
A link to a runbook with first mitigation steps
questions.explanation: Runbooks cut MTTR and stress, especially at night.

items.title: Chaos engineering
items.context: Chaos engineering runs controlled experiments — killing instances, injecting latency, cutting dependencies — to check that the system tolerates failures as designed. Start small, with a hypothesis and an abort plan, in staging before production.

questions.prompt: The point of chaos engineering is to:
choices: Find weaknesses through controlled failure experiments before real incidents do
questions.explanation: Netflix's Chaos Monkey popularised the idea.

items.title: Toil
items.context: In SRE terms, toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with load and has no lasting value. Google's SRE guidance caps toil at about 50% of an engineer's time; the rest goes to engineering that removes it.

choices: Manually restarting the same service every morning
questions.explanation: If a script could do it and it keeps coming back, it's toil.
